title: Project: messy export → report (with AI)
goal: Turn a messy sales export into a clean, checked city report: fix spaces, capitals and text-numbers, catch a duplicate order, summarise with UNIQUE, SUMIFS and COUNTIFS, and test an AI-suggested formula before you trust it.

steps.text:
Meena runs a home bakery in Pune and Mumbai. Her billing app just exported this week's orders, and it's a mess:

• Names have extra spaces and odd capitals.
• Amounts like ==D2== sit on the **left**. They're text, so SUM would skip them.
• Order **5002** shows up twice.

In this project you'll clean the export, check it, summarise it by city and polish the result, using what you've learned. There are no step-by-step instructions: you choose the tool. Clues are there if you get stuck.

steps.prompt: Start with the names. In ==E2==, clean the customer in `B2`: no stray spaces, and a capital letter at the start of each name.
steps.explain: `TRIM` removed the leading space and squashed the double gap; `PROPER` then turned `rohan MEHTA` into **Rohan Mehta**. You need both: either one alone leaves part of the mess.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Two jobs, so two functions: one removes the extra spaces, one fixes the capitals. Put one inside the other.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Look closely at the result: it should be exactly **Rohan Mehta**. `TRIM` alone leaves `MEHTA` shouting; `PROPER` alone keeps the spaces.

clues: `TRIM` fixes spaces, `PROPER` fixes capitals.
Nest them: `=PROPER(TRIM(B2))`.

steps.prompt: The city has the same trouble, plus a space at the front. In ==F2==, clean `C2`.
steps.explain: ` PUNE` became **Pune**. This matters later: SUMIFS treats `Pune` and `Pune ` (with a space) as two different cities and would split one total in half.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use the same pair as for the name: one for spaces, one for capitals.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The result should be **Pune**: capital P, no space in front. Is your formula fixing both the space and the capitals?

clues: You've already built this formula for `B2`.
Same two functions, pointed at `C2`.

steps.prompt: Now the amount. In ==G2==, turn the text in `D2` into a real number that SUM can add.
steps.explain: `450 ` was text with a space at the end; now **450** sits on the right as a real number. `VALUE` converts text that looks like a number, and `TRIM` clears any stray space first.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use **VALUE**: it converts text that looks like a number into a real one.

clues: There's a function whose name is the thing you want: the VALUE of the text.
Wrap `TRIM` inside it in case of spaces.

steps.prompt: `E2:G2` hold your three formulas, and `E2:G8` is selected. Copy the formulas down to every order with the keyboard.
clues: D is for down.

steps.prompt:
The clean columns are done, so we pasted them as plain **values** over the raw ones (Paste Special → Values keeps the answers and drops the formulas). Meena wants first names for thank-you notes. We typed `Rohan` in `E2`.

You're on `E3`. Fill in the rest from that one example.

On a Mac, Flash Fill is under **Data → Flash Fill**.
clues: E is for Excel guessing the pattern.
Hold Ctrl and tap E.

steps.prompt: Order 5002 looks familiar. In ==F5==, count how many times the order number in `A5` appears in the whole Order column.
steps.explain: **2**: order 5002 is in the list twice, so one of them is a repeat. Any count above 1 is a duplicate. Counting first lets you look before you delete (Data → Remove Duplicates).

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Count how often a value appears in a list: that's a COUNT with a condition.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Count `A5` across the **whole** column `A2:A8`, not just one row.

clues: Count the cells in `A2:A8` that equal `A5`.

steps.prompt: We deleted the second 5002 row and dropped the order numbers, so six orders are left. Meena wants one summary row per city. In ==E2==, list each city once with a single formula.
steps.explain: `Pune` is in `E2` and `Mumbai` spilled into `E3`. If a third city ever appears in the data, this list grows by itself.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: You want each city once: Excel has a function named for exactly that.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The list should be Pune and Mumbai, each once. Point the formula at the City column, `B2:B7`.

clues: The function name means “only one of each”.
Give it the City column `B2:B7`.

steps.prompt: How much did **Pune** bring in? In ==F2==, total the amounts for the city named in `E2`.
steps.explain: **2150**: Rohan 450 + Sara 1200 + Dev 500. Pointing at `E2` instead of typing “Pune” means the same formula can be copied down to Mumbai once its ranges are locked with `$`.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Add up the Amount column `C2:C7`, and look for the city in `B2:B7`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Only Pune's three orders should be added, not every order.

clues: Sum range first, then the City column, then the city to match.

steps.prompt: Meena gives a free gift for orders of **500 or more**. In ==G2==, count how many Pune orders earned one.
steps.explain: **2**: Sara's 1200 and Dev's 500. Dev's order is exactly 500, so `">=500"` counts it; `">500"` would miss him. Counting every 500+ order in the list would also give 3, because Mumbai has Meena's 850.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Two conditions at once: the city **and** the amount. That needs a COUNT with an S on the end.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Pune only, and 500 counts as “500 or more”: use `">=500"` with quotes.

clues: One pair of ranges for the city, another pair for the amount.
The amount test is `">=500"`.

steps.prompt: Meena asked an AI chatbot for **Mumbai's total**. It replied with the formula already in `F3` and sounded very sure, but the cell shows **0**. Fix the formula in ==F3==.
steps.explain: **1500**: Anil 300 + Meena 850 + Kiran 350. The AI swapped the arguments: SUMIFS wants the **sum range first**, then each criteria range. It tried to add the city names, got 0 and still looked confident. Always check an AI formula against a number you can work out by hand.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Check which range is being added and which is being searched.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Mumbai's three orders should total 1500. In SUMIFS the first range is the one that gets **added**.

clues: Which column holds the numbers to add?
Swap the first two ranges.

steps.prompt:
The AI also suggested `=COUNTIF(C2:C7,">500")` to count orders of **500 or more**. It returns 2, but you can see **three** such orders: 1200, 850 and 500.

What's wrong with the suggestion?
options: The range must include the header
steps.explain: Dev's order is exactly 500, and `>` means strictly more than. Boundary values are where AI formulas most often go quietly wrong, so always test one that sits right on the edge.
wrongFeedback: COUNTIF counts numbers happily. The difference is in the condition.
Headers don't matter here. Look at the condition instead.
clues: Which sign includes the number itself?

steps.prompt: Time to polish. The summary headings in `E1:G1` are selected. Make them stand out.
clues: B is for bold.

steps.prompt: The totals in `F2:F3` are selected. This report will go to Meena's accountant: make the big numbers easy to read.
clues: The key that adds thousands separators is Ctrl + Shift + 1.
